character_map.blurb: Two detectives — one in Fukuoka, one in Tokyo — piece together how an apparent love-suicide on a Kyushu beach was in fact a calculated double murder engineered to silence a government corruption linchpin. The crime is less a whodunit than a howdunit: the businessman responsible is visible from the opening pages, but his alibi, built on the precision of Japan's railway timetable, seems impregnable.
character_map.notes: Character map based on the verified analysis of Seichō Matsumoto's Tokyo Express (original title: Ten to Sen, 1958). Spoiler levels reflect the novel's structure as a howdunit: Yasuda's guilt is transparent early (level 1–2), while Ryoko's role as the actual administrator of the poison is the genuine climax revelation (level 3). The unprosecuted ending is treated as a level-3 thematic resolution.
character_map.title: Tokyo Express

factions.label: Fukuoka Police
factions.description: The regional force that first investigates the bodies found on Kashii Beach, inclined to close the case quickly as a love-suicide.

factions.label: Tokyo Metropolitan Police
factions.description: The Second Investigative Division, focused on white-collar crime, which assigns Mihara to the case after Tokyo connections emerge.

factions.label: Yasuda Household
factions.description: The industrialist and his wife at the centre of the conspiracy — a unit defined outwardly by wealth and status, inwardly by coercion and complicity.

factions.label: Unnamed Ministry (Government Corruption Network)
factions.description: The unnamed ministry and its officials whose procurement corruption Sayama facilitated as linchpin; their protection necessitates the murders.

factions.label: Koyuki Restaurant
factions.description: The Tokyo restaurant where Toki worked and Yasuda cultivated his government contacts; its staff serve as unwitting instruments in Yasuda's alibi construction.

character_map.subtitle: Seichō Matsumoto, 1958

characters.name: Torigai Jūtarō
characters.description: The first investigator on the scene, sharp-minded and unegotistical despite institutional pressure from his boss to close the case quickly. His private moral discomfort — not any systemic mandate — drives him to keep pulling at threads, making him a protagonist operating almost entirely against the grain of the institution he represents.
characters.name_evidence: Senior detective, Fukuoka Police, first investigator at Kashii Beach

characters.name: Kiichi Mihara
characters.role: Inspector, Tokyo Metropolitan Police (Second Investigative Division)
characters.description: The novel's second-half protagonist, younger and even more dedicated than Torigai, whose infectious enthusiasm for the case leads him across the entire rail network of Japan piecing together the timetable alibi. He is the one who ultimately authors the letter to Torigai laying out the full truth — a conclusion that is correct but unprosecutable.
characters.name_evidence: Young inspector, Second Investigative Division, Tokyo Metropolitan Police

characters.name: Tatsuo Yasuda
characters.description: A successful businessman normalised entirely by the postwar economic order — he did not become corrupt in any dramatic sense but simply cultivated government contacts as standard practice. He engineers the murders not out of personal passion but to protect a bribery network on which his business depends, constructing a timetable-precision alibi in Sapporo while his wife does the actual killing; his guilt is transparent early, yet he escapes prosecution, which is Matsumoto's point about how power protects itself.
characters.name_evidence: President of a precision tool company, regular patron at Koyuki, antagonist mastermind

characters.name: Ryoko Yasuda
characters.role: Wife of Yasuda; the person who physically committed the murders
characters.description: Simultaneously perpetrator and victim: a wealthy, educated, beautiful woman whose psychological subjugation to her husband is so complete that she participated in a double murder to preserve their marriage, tolerating his affairs and obeying his demands because his approval is the axis of her identity. The novel refuses to simplify her — she is neither a monster nor merely a tool — and her escape from prosecution is as troubling as her husband's.
characters.name_evidence: Wife of Tatsuo Yasuda; revealed to have administered the poison on the beach

characters.name: Kenichi Sayama
characters.role: Victim; government official and corruption linchpin
characters.description: An assistant section chief responsible for procurement and contracts who served as the invisible connective tissue between corrupt ministry officials and industrialists like Yasuda; his death is engineered precisely because, as linchpin, his removal collapses the public prosecutor's entire investigation into the bribery network.
characters.name_evidence: Assistant section chief at unnamed ministry, victim found on Kashii Beach

characters.name: Toki Kuwayama
characters.description: A waitress at the Koyuki who kept to herself and never flirted with customers, yet was the object of Yasuda's regular attention; her death is a collateral necessity of the cover story — she is killed to make the double suicide staging credible, making her murder the most nakedly utilitarian act in the novel.
characters.name_evidence: Waitress at Koyuki restaurant, victim found on Kashii Beach alongside Sayama

characters.name: Yaeko and Tomiko
characters.description: Two workers at the Koyuki whom Yasuda manoeuvres into accompanying him to Tokyo Station on October 14th, where they observe Toki and Sayama boarding the Asakaze Express — a manufactured sighting designed to establish the fiction of a lovers' journey to Kyushu and to give the alibi independent human witnesses.
characters.name_evidence: Two women working at Koyuki restaurant, witnesses Yasuda brings to Tokyo Station

characters.name: Unnamed Ministry officials / bribery scandal figures
characters.role: Government officials implicated in bribery scandal
characters.description: The unnamed ministry officials whose procurement corruption Sayama facilitated; individually unidentified in the novel's text, they form the systemic backdrop that makes the murders necessary and ensures no formal prosecution follows the detectives' discoveries.
characters.name_evidence: Corruption network Sayama served as linchpin for; members unnamed in source

character_map.coverage_note: All characters named in the analysis Cast section are included. The 'Unnamed Ministry officials / bribery scandal figures' entry is treated as a single collective character per schema rules, as the analysis explicitly notes their members are unnamed in the source. Yaeko and Tomiko are listed as a combined entry reflecting how the analysis presents them as a pair.

character_map.adaptation_note: The 1958 Toei film directed by Tsuneo Kobayashi follows the novel's plot mechanics faithfully — including the four-minute window and the Sapporo alibi — but flattens the moral complexity of Ryoko's character into a simpler 'weakling elegance' contrasted against a one-dimensionally cunning husband, losing the novel's refusal to reduce her to either pure victim or pure perpetrator. No significant divergences in the 2007 TV drama were documented in available sources.
character_map.setting_preamble: Post-war Japan, 1957–58. Japan's national railway network — its published timetables, station platforms, and dining-car receipts — functions as both the crime's mechanism and its central metaphor. The title's Japanese original, Ten to Sen ('Points and Lines'), names the geometry of alibi: fixed stations in time and space, connected by routes that can be weaponised by anyone who knows them precisely enough.
